A reader living in a small community in Virginia ( or was it West Virginia ?) wrote to me asking if I could get him some information concerning a Hebrew-Chris-tian revivalist named Jacob Gartenhaus , who represented himself to be either a Rabbi or a son of a Rabbi . I asked for information in this colmn and received the following letter from the gentleman himself from Atlanta , Ga . I give it exactly as it is written : The Home Mission Board SOUTHERN BAPTIST CONVENTION Atlanta , Ga . Department of Jewish Evangelism , Jacob Gartenhous , Evangelist . Mr . Charles H . Joseph , Care The Jewish Times , Baltimore , Md .</p><p dir="auto">Dear Sir : My attention has been called to a copy of the August 23 rd issue of the Jewish Times , in which a reader of Coeburn , Va ., asks for information concerning a Baptist , Jewish Evangelist , and since I happen to be that individual , I am happy to comply with your correspondent s and your wishes and am therefore herewith enclosing a brief biography of my life , published by the Moody Bible Institue of Chicago . It has ever been the policy of the editors of Jewish papers to speak of their brethren , who have accepted the principals of Christ , in a most questionable and injurious manner , even though many of us would gladly give our lives if we could , by so doing , save our brethren . To illustrate the fact that we are ever ready to help our brethren , when Queen Marie of Roumania visited Baltimore , at the time when our brethren were suffering much persecution in her country , the Baptists of Maryland were holding their annual State Convention . I presented a resolution , which was unanimously passed by that body of people , urging the Queen to use her influence and put an end to such persecution . That resolution was published by practically all of the daily papers in the United States . Happily , soon after , the condition of our brethren across the sea improved and i should like to think that I had a small part . This may satisfy the curiosity of your correspondent . If he , or any other , desires any further information , I should be happy to furnish same . Sincerely yours , JG : H Jacob Gartenhaus . I have only a single comment to make on the foregoing and that is that Evangelist Gartenhaus pays himself too high a compliment if he believes for a moment that he had the slightest influence in changing Roumania s policy toward the Jews . The fact is that long after the Queen returned home outrages continued to such a degree that protests were launched by Rabbi Stephen Wise , the late Louis Marshall and others . Diplomatic conferences were held by Jewish leaders and Roumanias representatives in this country . As a result of all this there has been only a slight improvement in Jewish conditions in Roumania . Oh , I forgot ! Space prevents the publication of Evangelist Gartenhaus life but he states he was born in Austria and it was the cherished hope of his parents that he would become a Rabbi . He tells of a restless urge toward wanderlust and the hardships he endured when he left home and wandered from city to city until he reached Berlin . Finally he decided to leave for America . He says that his brother was student in a Hebrew Seminary and he , too , through finding the New Testament , decided to become a Christian . They both came to this country and Jacob entered the Moody Bible Institute in Chicago and became a full-fledged missionary to the Jews . Louis Marshall was a great leader in Jewry . I never knew a man whose profession lay outside Jewish life who</p><p dir="auto">gave so much of his energy and his time to Jewish life . He was an indomitable fighter and a tireless worker for his people . No phase of Jewish life left him untouched . He took himself and his work seriously . While he was by no means an orator yet the sincerity of his messages always held profound interest for . his hearers . The devotion to every worthy Jewish cause made him respected as few Jews have been in recent times and lent tremendous weight to every appeal he made for his people . He never used what Roosevelt called weasel words . He hit straight from the shoulder and used the Biggest Stick he could find . I remember how Ford hit the ceiling when he received Marshalls telegram shortly after he started his infamous campaign against the Jews . It was said that Marshall s words angered him more and stung more acutely than tons of criticism that were launched on him afterward . It was strange that the very man who aroused his ire should be the one to whom Ford turned when he decided that he wanted to apologize and to retract to the world and to the Jewish people . Fords confession was Marshall s . This merely serves to show the commanding positions he occupied as leader of American Jewry and that it was so recognized by the world at large as well as by Jewry . Whenever I used to read one of Mr . Marshall s scorching letters to an individual who had in his opinion championed intolerance I used to think of Lincoln who vowed that every time that thing ( slavery ) raised its head he would whack it every opportunity he got . So Louis Marshall determined to hit intolerance wherever it stuck its ugly head , even though it rested on the shoulders of an important individual . It would be impossible to mention even the names of those with whom he took issue on matters of Jewish interest . And when he wrote a letter of criticism the one who received it felt it because Marshall knew how to arrange his facts and drive home his points . He undoubtedly felt deeply as a Jew because he had the passion of a crusader in fighting those he felt had injured his people . It seems strange to me now that I think of it that I should have met Louis Marshall only once in all the years that he was before the Jewish public . We had exchanged many letters and on more than one occasion he took the opportunity of bringing me to book for some statement which he felt I should not have made . While I could not always agree with him I had an abiding faith in his honesty and I had for him the highest respect as a man and as a Jew . I question whether we have anyone in America today who can take his place ? He was a forceful personality and in his death , world Jewry has lost one of its most valuable members . JEWS HELD FOR MURDER Charged with murder by premeditated shooting , forty-four Jews have been imprisoned in the citadel of Acre , where Vladimir Jabotinsky and nineteen of his co-defenders of Jerusalem were confined in 1920 . Their release on bail is impossible before a magistrate decides under which charge they shall be held . These forty-four men were captured in the flour mill of Haifa during the riots . They are reported to be in excellent spirits and do not complain against the ill treatment which they suffer at the hands of the wardens . They are being supplied with food by the workers of the Haifa kitchen . JERUSALEM AFTER THE MASSACRE ( Continued from Page 2 ) Frederick H . Kisch . At Tiberias , despite a local peace pact , I found a hysterical , nervous strain , although the peace was preserved . But at Migdal there were several cases of incendiarism and robbery . There , too , the military protection is imperfect , the Commanding Officer wrongly accusing the Jews of giving false alarms . Safed is plunged in mourning and bewilderment . I saw many Jews , who but yesterday were well-to-do , standing in the bread lines . Dozens who left their homes to seek protection at the Governor s house , returned thirty-six hours later to find everything destroyed . All they have left in the world are the clothes in which they stand . The looted and burned houses present a ghastly sight . Looting continued for thirty hours after the massacre . For several days before the attack the local police commander , Farraday , fainly implored for military help . The old type of Jew in the town asks , dazed : Why was Turkey able to preserve our lives and property , but England is not ? Yesod Hamaaleh was completely robbed . No casualties occurred there . The spirit among the youth , the pioneers in the colonies in the Emek and Upper Galilee , is astounding . At Beth Alpha , which withstood five attacks , they are indomitable and unshaken . Not one Jew fell during the defense of the colony , but there were many casualties among the Arab attackers . Encouraging as this may be for the present , it may not be a guarantee of future peace , as the Bedouins , true to their ancient tradition , may seek revenge for each of their tribe killed . This creates a dangerous position for the Beth Alpha settlers , but not one of them is willing or prepared to quit . Kfar Gileadi and Tel Hai , which were not attacked , stand unafraid . One colony , asked if military help is needed , replied proudly in the negative . In Metullah , the sculptor Melnikoss is calmly contin</p><p dir="auto">uing his work on the statue of Joseph Trumpeldor , pioneer here , who died in defense of the Galilee colony Tel Hai . In Degania , as elsewhere , guards are needed . It is impossible to carry out work in the fields , such as irrigation and weeding where the settlers would have to work away from the group . This will result in damage for the crop . The interference with regular shipment of produce will also cause losses . Bananas and other goods , ready for shipment , are beginning to rot . Sir John Chancellor s second proclamation produced a bad effect . The impression of an incomprehensible vacillation has left the Yishub startled and disappointed . * * * JEWS RETURNING TO SAFED Jerusalem —( J . T . A . )—The Jewish population of a Safed is gradually returning to the city where they are staying in the protected area which is being daily enlarged . A portion of the Jewish quarter , which was destroyed by fire is uninhabitable . Relief work is being organized by the Jewish Agency with the aid of funds received from the Palestine Emergency Fund in the United States and other countries . In many instances the attackers were recognized as the former Arab neighbors of the Jewish residents who were on friendly relations for many years , a situation which is distressing . Some 90 Arabs were arrested in Safed on the charge of assault and looting . An English missionary , Dr . Semple . declared that the looting continued in Safed until the following afternoon . The trials have not yet been started . Col . Frederick H . Kisch , chairman of the Zionist Executive in Jerusalem , who is travelling throughout the country together with Mr . Maurico Samuel , well-known American novelist and Zionist , visited Safed and the upper Galilean colonies up to Metulla . He reports that all is quiet now and that the Jewish settlers are in good spirits , except for the difficulties they encounter in arranging for proper self-protection in places where the protection of the military authorities has not yet been secured . Members of the Jewish self-defense body in the colony Yavneel , who were arrested by the authorities several days ago , were released . A survey of conditions in the Jewish agricultural settlements throughout the country made by representatives of the Zionist Executive , showed that with the exception of one settler killed in Hulda and two in Beer Tuvia , no other casualties occurred in the agricultural settlements in the country notwithstanding the numerous attacks made on the settlements throughout Palestine . The Jewish settlements were protected by the settlers self-defense . Arab policemen were appointed to participate in the inquiry into the Safed massacre . The Jewish population of Safed will not submit evidence to those who were active in the pogrom on that city , the government was informed bv the Jews of the city . Jewish or English investigators were demanded . Sixty Arabs were arrested in the villages which participated in the attack on the colony Kastinia . Among the arrested are two sheiks . Troops discovered the looters of the colony Kfar Tabor , who drove off the cattle of the colonists . Ten Bedouins were killed and a soldier wounded in the skirmish when the troops attempted to recapture the cattle . All consuls are actively collecting material concerning their nationals who suffered in the outbreak . The French Consul visited the Tel Aviv municipality . He expressed his indignation at the outrages perpetrated by the Arabs . Assaults on individual Jews are continuing at Haifa . Much to the surprise of the Jewish community , the</p><p dir="auto">Jewish engineer Miller , whose house was burned to the ground , was arrested . Miller was charged with firing from his house . The arrest of 31 Jews at the Rothschild Grands Moulins also caused surprise . When their barracks were burned by the Arab marauders the 31 found refuge in the flour mill . Among the wounded at Safed was Salin Cohen , Persian Vice-Consul . * * * The Jews of Acre have decided to evacuate the town , proceeding to Haifa . The decision to evacuate came after the few remaining families were stoned by their neighbors last Friday . The only Jews remaining in Acre are 48 prisoners held at the citadel . They were arrested in the flour mill where they had organized for self-defense . The presiding judge of the court informed the prisoners he will not try a single man until he has examined all documents . * * * MILLION DOLLARS NEEDED IMMEDIATELY Jerusalem —( J . T . A . )—A preliminary estimate of the Jewish damages caused by the Moslem Arab attacks during the last fortnight , made by the Zionist Executive , shows that the damages amount to several million dollars . One thousand families who were formerly well-to-do , are now homeless and reduced to utter destitution . It was estimated that the amount of one million dollars will be required immediately for their rehabilitation . Fifteen hundred refugees from the nearby Jewish colonies , Hebron , Gaza and other centers are now in TelAviv . The school houses were thrown open to provide them with temporary shelter . A special relief committee is at work distributing food . The Women s International Zionist Organization and the Hadassah , American Women Zionist Organization , are extending medical and social aid . Shop Employees' Facility. All the shops from the Russian Buildings to the Jaffa Gate, on both sides of the main street, have agreed to close down at 7 o'clock. Previously shopclosing hours Were as late as eight and nine p.m. It is surprising that an ordinance of the type of the Early Closing Act in England cannot be devised for Palestine. Shop assistants are an overworked tribe. They labour far ten, eleven and twelve hours at a most unmittgating activity, are constantly on their feet and do not enjoy the best of conditions. It is very rarely, except on the Sabbaths, that a shop assistant can get a half-holiday, and while the 7 o'clock closing agreement will alleviate his lot, the shop assistant still will have to work hard in order to keep going. An official closing day during the week, infringement of which would be punishable by law, would certainly be a great step forward in ameliorating the condition of shop employees although exceptions might be made in certain ases where tourist trade is concerned. Higher Postage for England. Announcement has been made by the General Post Office authorities here that as from March 1st, 1929, postage to England will be raised to 13 mils for ordinary correspondence, with a charge of 7 mils for each additional 20 grammes. This represents an increase of almost 100 per cent, in the present postage rates. It is regrettable that the General Post Office has not seen fit to issue a communique upon a matter which has caused a good deal of comment throughout the country. Particularly interesting is it that at a time when in England a movement is on foot, and a Bill in consideration of Parliment, to re-institute penny postage for the inland service, a contrary step should have been taken in a British Mandatory country. The reason obviously is the small margin which the present 7-mil postage has afforded for the operation of the service; but one would have expected a far lower than a IpO per cent, increase. No doubt the Post Office authorities are trying to raise as large a reserve fund as possible for the building which they are said to be contemplating on the vacant site in front of the present Y.M.C A. quarters. It is hoped that this is the case, and that the additional charge on correspondence with Great Britain will at least have the compensating factor of establishing some permanent monument to the uncomplaining users of the postal service who have to bear the cost. <p dir="auto">Jewish National Council Memorandum</p><p dir="auto">This year's memorandum addressed to the Permanent Mandates Commission of the League of Nations at Genieva by the General Council of the Jewish Community of Palestine (Vaad Leumi) is like previous memoranda submitted in past years, couched in strong criticism of the Mandatory Government. It is an 84-page document a little under foolscap size, printed in English and Hebrew, and the principal part of its contents makes up a detailed commentary upon the Hope-Simpson Report of October, 1930, whicli the Council tries to prove is fallacious and arrives at wrong conclusions. The Council starts by referring to its June, 1930, memorandum and quotes the section stating that "the Government (of Palestine) have often taken a position which is tantamount to refusing members of the Jewish community that civil equality which is guaranteed to national minorities even, in countries in whicli declarations for the establishment of a National Home form no part of the public policy of the land." The Council recalls that it stated that although "the Jews of Palestine constituted 20 per cent of the settled population, they have been paying nearly 45 per cent of its revenue, and receiving back only 14 per cent of Government expenditure on education, less than TO per cent of the expenditure fn public /he Illi ,and no more than 10 per cent of public works expenditure." Immgration Restrictions. Embargoes on immigration are stressed. Although the Palestine Immigration Ordinance, 1925. provided that the minimum, capital to be produced on demand by an immigrant of independent means was £500. it is stated, legislation passed by the Government of Palestine on April 2nd raised this amount to £1,000. "Tris restriction is justified neither by economic conditions in th? w. rid and especially in centres of Jewish emigration, nor by the economic conditions prevailing in the country for the</p><p dir="auto">absorption of immigrants of this class. In fact the substantial fall in the Cost of Living Index in the country facilitates the absorption of people of more limited means than was the case during the period 202526." Finally, in concluding its observations upon its past memorandum, the Vaad Leumi states that nothing has been done "to encourage close settlement by Jews on the land including State Lands and waste lands" as provided for in the Mandate. During the period under review "the policy of the local Administration has continued unchanged," states the memorandum, which last year had charged the Government that "the disturbances of August, 1929, the conduct of the Government during those disturbances, the Report of the Shaw Commission with its all too obvious tendency to exonerate the instigators from any guilt for the bloodshed which occurred as a result of their instigation, that all this and much more was the inevitable consequence of a policy of opposition to the Jewish National Home which some members of the Palestine Administration have been pursuing now for many years." Discouraging Immigration. That the Department of Immigration has continued' not to function as a department for the encouragement of immigration, but as one for its discouragement, is the next charge made. Jewish tourists with adequate means who, after coming to observe conditions in the country, decide to remain, meet with great difficulties in their endeavours to obtain permission to stay in Palestine. Members of liberal professions who, while visiting the country were given definite offers of employment to local institutions, have been refused permission to remain. The memorandum then accuses the Chief Immigration Officer as using his discretion on applications by prospective immigrants and tourists wishing to remain in a too arbitrary manner, and. only recently, of demonstratin'!</p><p dir="auto">through the Department its "usual attitude of contempt towards the representations of the Jewish Agency and the Jewish Community of Palestine" in connection with the preparation of the Labour Schedule for the half-year (April-September, 1931). "Although a very conservative quota was prepared, with great care and after a. thorough examination of labour conditions in the country, it was curtailed by the Government to a ludicrous minimum," it is charged. Th tirade against the Palestine Government goes on to public health expenditure. The Government contribution actually amounts to one seventh of the total education expenditure of the Government although the Jewish population constitutes twenty per cent, of the settled population in the country. The Jewish medical institutions continue to bear almost the entire cost of the maintenance of the Jewish health service which caters for the members of the Jewish community. The Hadassah (the Women Zionist Organisation of America) alone has spent no less than five million dollars in Palestine during the last ten years. This expenditure has enabled the Government : (a) to reduce their expenditure on the health services to the utmost possible limit; (b) to allocate the bulk of their health budget to the service of the Arab population. "Altho the population of Palestine has increased during the period 192129 by about 200,000 and the expenditure of the Government by about £800,000. the allocation to -the Department of Health has decreased during the same period by some £45,000. This reduction would have been impossible but for the liberal contribution made by the Jewish Agency, and especially the Hadassah, towards the upkeep of a health service for the Jewish community, and the equally substantial sums, amountinng to no less than £300.000. expended by the various Jewish colonisation agencies for the sanitation of the country." Out of a total of 19.546 Jewish in-patients in all Palestine hospitals 01 1929, only 511 were treated in Government hospitals and in hospit-</p><p dir="auto">als subsidised by the Government, and these were for the most part policemen or other officials. Only 83 out of a total 1,709 in-patients in the Central Government Hospital in Jerusalem were Jews. This represents 5 per cent of the total, altho Jews constitute two-thirds of the population of Jerusalem, it is averred. No Social Legislation. Another failing of the Government which is underscored is that no social legislation was passed in the year. The High Commissioner rejected the proposals made by the Executive Committee of the Federation of Jewish Labour with regard to laws for the compulsory health insurance &lt;f workers. Similarly there was no progress made in the development of local government, the Council points oufNow, as before, the city government of Jerusalem, the capital of the country, continues without the participation of representatives of the Jews, who constitute two-thirds of its population and contribute 80 per cent of its revenue. "The causes which prompted the Jewish councilors to withdraw from the Municipal Council still obtain, and Government have done nothing to remove them,''' it is said. The peace and protection of the Jewish community are by no means assured, resumes the memorandum, which refers to the murder of Jewish settlers at Yadjur, near Haifa, when when they were ambushed by brigands who have not yet been traced. The Council claims that the promised reorganisation of the Palestine constabulary, and the addition of more Jewish policemen, has not been carried out, and that no measures have been taken to provide arms as protection for outlying Jewish settlements. "On the other hand," runs the plaint, "the Arabs of Palestine have unlimited possibilities of securing arms of an effective type in large quantities and with great ease. Transordan on the one side and the South of Palestine on the other side, both areas under the jurisdiction of the British Mandatory, are territories in which there is an unrestricted traffic in arms, and there can be no possible check on the penetration of</p><p dir="auto">such arms from either of these territories to other parts of Palestine. Any unrest which might result from the religious, racial or political instigation which is at work especially in connection with the frequent religious celebrations held in Palestine such as Nebi Mussa, Nebi Saleh, Nebi Rubin, &amp;c,, is likely to inefte fanatic crowds to acts of violence. Under these circumstances, the feeling of insecurity among the Jewish community is explicable and justified, 4 specially when it is remembered that they are denied adequate means of protection." Failure of Trade Boycott. The next section relates to the failure of the economic boycott promoted by the instigators "responsible for the disturbances of August 1929 who had hoped to shake the economic foundations of the Jewish community/' The Jewish community successfully overcome all the economic consequences of the disturbances thanks to the generous measures of relief extended by World Jewry for the reconstruction, it is asseverated, "but what the boycott and riots failed to achieve was achieved by the political restrictions that came close in their wake in the period that followed." The Council then cites the Shaw Commission Report and the statements of Jewish labour immigration, "have seriously shaken the confidence of Jews in the policy of the British Government." The policy of the Government, die political development, had a most depressing effect on the Influx of fresh capital and on the economic tftuation generally. Signs</p><p dir="auto">of economic hardship began to make themselves felt in May, 1930, immediately after the suspension of Jewish immigration. Criticing a British Expert. The remainder of the Memorandum is taken up with a close and searching analysis of the Hope simpson Report, published in October 1930, on Immigration, Land Settlement and Development, which served as the basis of the British White Paper "in which an attempt was made to validate and justify all th^ restrictions which had been imposed on Jewisli enterprise in direct contradiction to the provisions of the Mandate, and to add many more to their number.'' Both the Jews of Palestine and of the world over have regarded that policy as "a pronouncement which most ruthlessly curtails and hinders all work for the reconstruction of Palestine by the Jewish people and as an attempt to put a stop to all creative work by Jews in their historic homeland, to hold up Jewish immigration and prevent all acquisition of land by Jewish immigration for their own settlement. The Council of the Jews of Palestine demands that "the gates of the country be opened to Jewish immigrations who shall be admitted not as alien immigrants but as sons repatriated to their country." It is the Council's "firm and sincere conviction that this right of the Jewish people in Palestine docs not in the least way prejudice the rights of the Arabs to their full economic and cultural development." Palestine Has a Future. In its full criticism of the Simp-</p><p dir="auto">son report, the Council has divided its analysis into several parts: The Agricultural Absorptive Capacity of Palestine, the Cultivable Area, the Absorptive Capacity of Urban Centres, Jewish Immigration and the Arab Worker, and Jewish Settlement and the Fellah. In the latter part, it points out the conflicting views of the two British Commissioners, — Sir John Hope Simpson who had attributed the peasants' plight to the shortage of land, and Mr. C. F. Strickland who" investigated the possibilities of introducing Agricultural Co-operation among the Palestinian Arab villagers) who said their economic difficulties were due to the usurious rates of interest on loans extorted by the big Moslem Effendis, or landlords. The conclusions arrived at by the commentators on the Simpson report are worthy of reprinting, for they utterly controvert the statements made by Hope-Simpson. (1) The most reliable estimate tor the cultivable area of Palestine, leaving the Beersheba region out of account, is 10,500,000 dunams. (2) Thore are large areas in the Beersheba region capable of cultivation if the problem of irrigation is solved. This should be taken in hand. (3) In spite of the fact that Transjordan holds rich reserves of irrigable land, Jewish settlement is not allowed there. This is discriminatory and contrary to the principle of civil equality. (4) The total area of the land actually under cultivation in Palestine is 5-516million dunams. This means</p><p dir="auto">that, excluding Transjordan and the Beersheba section, there are five million dunams of uncultivated but cultivable land. (5) The development of this area alone will absorb an additional 55,000 70,000 agricultural families. (6) With the development of the latest agricultural possibilities of Palestine, the country can support an additional 100,000 families without taking into consideration either Transjordan or the South. (7) By thorough reclamation and development in Palestine and the South it will be possible considerably to increase this number of new settlers. (8) The extent of State lands now available is limited, having been for the most part distributed by the Government to Arabs in hundreds and even thousands of dunams per family. which is far in excess of what is equitable. (9) The lands thus granted, too large for the owners to work, are now being openly sold, but inasmuch as the purchase price has not yet been fully paid to the Government, the land is still vested in the Government. so that the inequitable distribution may still be remedied. 10) The root of the fellah's evil plight lies not in lack of land but in his burden of debt and the usury of the Effendis. The fellah must pay usurious rates of interest out of his meagre income, while the tenant cultivator with no land of his own suffers from the additional burden of grossly exaggerated rents. (11) There are considerable prospects of industrial development in</p><p dir="auto">Palestine; special attention should be paid to the possibilities of the development of the textiles, chemicals, canning industries, &amp;c. (12) The geographical situation of Palestine, its proximity to the markets of the Middle East and the Suez Canal, the Haifa Harbour now being constructed and the Baghdad-Haifa line, all these clearly indicate that, given the existence in Palestine of a large enterprising population, the country will develop into an industrial centre for the whole of this vast hinterland. (13) The annual immigration, therefore, of some tens of thousands of people whose only hope of salvation is in Palestine, does not lie outside the true scope of the country. (14) The encouragement of such large-scale immigration neither prejudices the civil rights nor causes harm to the economic welfare of the present population of Palestine. Colonisation will expand the absorptive possibilities of agriculture, while the influx of capital for the purchase of land', the introduction of progressive methods of cultivation and the development of Arab co-operation on the model of Jewish co-operation, these and these alone will improve the condition and standard of life of the Arab cultivator. The immigrants with a standard of living considerably higher than that of the Arab workers who secure employment in the urban centres, do not dispossess or oust Arab workers: for their absorption is made possible only by those enterprises the establishment of which is inconceivable without the intensification of Jewish immigration and colo-</p><p dir="auto">(15) In this respect the efteet of ''new" colonisation are not to be distinguished from those of "old" colonisation, (i.e. Pre-War and Post-War Settlement.) The attempts to discriminate between them are unjustified, because they are not founded on fact. They originate from the hostility of those opponents to Zionism who find themselves constrained to admit the Ixmeficial effects of Jewish colonisation on the position of the Arabs in Palestine. (16) While Jewish enterprise naturally inclines mainly to the employment of Jews, Arabs form 20% of the total number of workers in Jewish employ. As against this, Arab establishments employ practically no Jews whatever. Moreover, the number of Jewish workers on Government and Municipal works is reduced to the lowest possible level even to their total exclusion in man, cases. This exclusion which is in effect a boycott, provides additional evidence of a Government policy calculated to ignore the interests of the Jewish community in all its needs —cultural, economic and colonisator, . (17) We are forced to the conclusion that the Development Scheme put forward by Sir John Hope Simpson in his report is based on premises and assumptions which have no foundation in fact, for which reason it is superfluous to enter into anny detailed analysis. Such are the seventeen conclusions of the General Council of Palestine Jewry. They are contradictions of the main arguments advanced in the Simpson Report. The sharpness of tone and condemning strictures of the</p><p dir="auto">whole Memorandum has been adopted by the Council with a view to stinging the Palatine or British Governments, apparantly, into retorting to the accusations. The Arabs have also submitted a memorandum to the l^eague of Nations, but it consists entirely of the Reply to the British White Paper and Simpson Report of 1930, published some months ago, and has already been given prominence in the world Press. HAIFA HARBOUR WORKS Since the publication of the last report considerable progress has been made on the Haifa Harbour, an official communique states. The Main Breakwater continue to be the chief item of work at present under construction. It has now advanced more than 1500 metres seaward and a depth of nearly 10 metres of water has been reached. A Pillar Crane was specially designed and built for the purpose of coping with the increasing dimensions of the breakwater as it advances seawards. This Crane was erected on the site and was brought into commission about the middle of December 1930. It is an efficient machine and its ca parity is equal to all the demands made on it. During January last an exceptionally severe storm occurred and the Main Breakwater was put to a crucial test through which it passed in a satisfactory manner. No damage was done to the Permanent Works or to the Pillar Crane. Temporary service Railways were displaced by the heavy seas, as were a number of trucks laden with stone. In spite of this,</p><p dir="auto">normal operations were quickly resumed. The Blockyard in the neighbourhood of the Old German Pier has been in commission for some time, and already a number of concrete blocKs for the main wharf wall have been cast. It will however be a little time yet before work at the Blockyard is in full swing. The Bubble Dyke, which forms the western side of the reclamation area has advanced to a point 768 metres from the shore. Preliminary works for the commencement of the construction of the main wharf wall have been carried out. These comprise the staging supported on timber piles upon which a 15-ton Derrick Crane is erected for the building by divers of the Central Abutment. Before this can be done however, a trench will have to be dredged down to the required foundation. The dredging is about to begin. A commencement has been made with the construction of the Lee Breakwater; stone being unloaded by trucks from the shore as well as deposited in the water by barges. The Quarries near Athlit, from which the whole of the stone for the breakwaters and other works is produced, have nearly reached their full output, and 8 to 10 trains of stone are being hauled each day from the Quarries to Carmel by the Palestine Railways.</p>
